clue.text: Like VS Naipaul's In A Free State: and is it new?

indicators.note: the book title read literally says the words are set free, so the letters of the words after the colon are rearranged

explanation.surface: A reader wonders whether Naipaul's Booker-winning book of stories brings anything new.
explanation.walkthrough: The book title doubles as the anagram signal: 'In A Free State' frees the letters of AND IS IT NEW. Naipaul was born in Trinidad.
explanation.definitionFit: Naipaul was a Trinidad-born writer of Indian descent, from the Caribbean islands.

clue.text: Drops of nice English sherry Herbert George drinks for good health

indicators.note: someone who drinks takes liquid inside, so one piece goes inside the writer's surname

parts.note: Herbert George were the given names of the novelist H. G. Wells

indicators.note: a drop is a small first taste, so only the opening letter of each of the next three words is taken

explanation.surface: The author of The Time Machine sips a pleasant English sherry, claiming it is for his health.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is the modern lifestyle term for being in sound physical and mental condition.

clue.text: Legendary seafarer's ill, twice having trouble among others at sea

parts.note: ill as a noun means a wrong, a sin
ill read a second time, now as an adjective meaning bad

indicators.note: among means surrounded by, so the trouble goes inside the jumbled letters
at sea means confused, so the letters of others are jumbled

parts.note: to ail is to trouble, as in what ails you

explanation.surface: A sailor of legend falls sick and twice gets into difficulty with the rest of the crew out on the ocean.
explanation.walkthrough: 'twice' tells you to read 'ill' in two senses, as a noun and as an adjective, and 'having' merely joins the two halves.
explanation.definitionFit: The Arabian Nights voyager made seven fabled journeys by ship.

clue.text: Children's edition

definitions.meaning: offspring, as in dying without heirs
a number of a periodical, as in this month's copy

explanation.definitionFit: The word covers both a person's offspring and one printing of a magazine.

clue.text: Extreme sort of irony when mother's disguised as son

indicators.note: something disguised as another thing takes its place, so the mother is swapped for the son

parts.note: dramatic irony is the kind where the audience knows more than the characters
ma is an informal word for mother
s is the standard abbreviation for son, as in family trees

explanation.surface: A stage farce reaches an extreme ironic twist when a mother turns up dressed as her own son.
explanation.walkthrough: Swapping MA for S in DRAMATIC leaves DRASTIC.
explanation.definitionFit: Drastic measures are severe and far-reaching, an adjective synonym.

clue.text: Ever-popular, like Peter Pan maybe

definitions.meaning: never going out of fashion, timeless in appeal
Peter Pan is the boy who never grows older

explanation.definitionFit: A classic never dates, and the boy who would not grow up never shows the years.

clue.text: Counterfeit Rushdie book's missing denoument

indicators.note: missing its ending means the final letter of the title is dropped

parts.note: Shame is a 1983 novel by Salman Rushdie

explanation.surface: A fake copy of a Rushdie novel is found to have lost its final pages.
explanation.walkthrough: Drop the last letter of SHAME. The clue prints 'denoument' for denouement, the closing stretch of a story.
explanation.definitionFit: A counterfeit is a fake, a pretence passed off as real.

clue.text: Novella originally serialised in obscure organ?

definitions.text: Novella originally serialised in obscure organ?

parts.words: Novella originally serialised in obscure organ?
parts.note: read the end as a riddle: the organ is the vital one in the chest, and obscure means dim, so this is a phrase for the middle of the gloom; the novella first appeared in instalments in Blackwood's Magazine, an organ in the sense of a periodical

explanation.surface: A short novel first came out in parts in some little-known magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'organ' looks like a magazine (a party organ); it is also the body's pump, sitting within the dark. Conrad's novella ran in Blackwood's Magazine in 1899.
explanation.definitionFit: Joseph Conrad's tale of a Congo voyage is a famous short novel first published in three parts.

clue.text: King's work is opening motorway; Earl, railway

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its first letter, here of the road

explanation.surface: A royal project to open a new motorway, with an earl cutting the ribbon on a railway too.
explanation.walkthrough: 'King' is Stephen King, not a monarch; his novel of a captive writer gives the answer. M, then IS, then E and RY.
explanation.definitionFit: Stephen King's 1987 novel is about a novelist held prisoner by an obsessive fan.

clue.text: Scattered diaspora's account of a better place

indicators.note: scattered means spread about, so the letters of the next word are rearranged

parts.note: the 's only shows possession or stands for 'is', so it adds no letters: the word before it gives these letters as it is written

explanation.surface: A people scattered far from home tell stories of a happier land.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scattered' looks like part of the meaning of diaspora, but it tells you to rearrange its letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The third part of Dante's Divine Comedy describes Heaven, the best place of all.

clue.text: Constable perhaps secures hat with last bit of tape

parts.note: to land a job or a fish is to secure it
a cap is a kind of hat

indicators.note: the last bit of a word is its final letter

explanation.surface: A police constable fastens his helmet with the tail end of some sticky tape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Constable' is not a policeman but John Constable, the English painter of rural scenes.
explanation.definitionFit: John Constable painted rural English views, so his canvases are pictures of countryside.

clue.text: Sci-fi humorist's manuscript following Byron's daughter

indicators.note: following means coming after, so the manuscript is placed after the daughter

parts.note: Ada Lovelace, the computing pioneer, was Lord Byron's daughter

explanation.surface: A comic science-fiction writer's manuscript comes after Byron's daughter in the library catalogue.
explanation.walkthrough: Douglas Adams wrote The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy.
explanation.definitionFit: Douglas Adams was a comic writer of science fiction, the creator of The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy.

clue.text: Some of those in line are standing extremely close

indicators.note: some of means only part of the following words is used, a run of letters inside them

explanation.surface: Some people in a queue stand very close together.
explanation.walkthrough: The run sits across liNE ARE STanding.
explanation.definitionFit: The superlative of near means closest of all, so extremely close.

clue.text: Old thesp's Shylock?

parts.note: ex means former, as in ex-wife
a thesp is a thespian, a performer on stage

explanation.surface: A retired performer once played Shylock.
explanation.walkthrough: Shylock seems to be a role the old actor played, but he defines the answer: he demands his pound of flesh.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's moneylender insists ruthlessly on his bond, the type of someone who demands payment.

clue.text: Architect's rough pen sketch is very emphatic

indicators.note: rough means unpolished or crude, so the letters of the words are put into a new order

parts.note: ff, fortissimo, is the musical marking for very loud

explanation.surface: An architect's quick pen drawing is boldly drawn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rough' shuffles PEN SKETCH IS. Seth Pecksniff is the hypocritical architect in Dickens's Martin Chuzzlewit.
explanation.definitionFit: Dickens made Pecksniff an architect who takes in pupils, though he designs nothing himself.

clue.text: Ayres, maybe with a measure of acidity, tolerated Paine's output?

parts.note: Pam Ayres is a popular English comic poet
pH is the scale for acidity
to let is to allow or tolerate

explanation.surface: A comic poet, with a sharp tongue, puts up with the writings of the radical Tom Paine.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Paine's Common Sense (1776) was a short booklet that stirred the American Revolution.
explanation.definitionFit: Paine wrote short political tracts, so a booklet was his typical work.

clue.text: Princess taking years off? It's quite possible

parts.note: Princess Ida is the title heroine of a Gilbert and Sullivan opera

indicators.note: off means wrong or not right, so the letters of years are jumbled

explanation.surface: Is a princess knocking a few years off her age? Very likely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taking years off' suggests a princess shaving her age; Ida is the title heroine of Gilbert and Sullivan's Princess Ida.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a conversational way to concede that something may well be true.

clue.text: Extra features in women's magazine about a case from retired crime writer

indicators.note: a thing that features in another appears inside it, so the extra goes inside the magazine

parts.note: Elle is a women's fashion magazine
more means extra, as in some more
on means about, as in a book on birds

indicators.note: the case of a word is its outside, its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A women's magazine runs bonus features about a case from a former detective-story writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retired' looks like the writer's status but gives the outer letters RD.
explanation.definitionFit: Elmore Leonard wrote crime novels such as Get Shorty and Out of Sight.

clue.text: Children's writer did work in modern voice, well suited to my tastes

parts.note: ran means operated, as a machine runs or works

parts.words: in modern voice, well suited to my tastes
parts.note: in current slang some means excellent, as in that's some car

explanation.surface: An author for young people worked in a contemporary style that suits me nicely.
explanation.walkthrough: Arthur Ransome wrote Swallows and Amazons.
explanation.definitionFit: Arthur Ransome wrote the Swallows and Amazons sailing stories for young readers.

clue.text: Essayist rewrote regularly, attaining a degree of brilliance

parts.note: Charles Lamb wrote the Essays of Elia

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is taken

explanation.surface: An essayist kept redrafting until his prose shone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly' takes the 2nd, 4th and 6th letters of REWROTE: ERT.
explanation.definitionFit: The lambert is a unit of luminance, a measure of how brightly a surface shines.

clue.text: Shake a bit of reluctance out of Lionel?

indicators.note: out of means taken away from, so a letter is removed from the surname

parts.note: Lionel Shriver is the author of We Need to Talk About Kevin

indicators.note: a bit of a word is here its first letter

explanation.surface: Shake off a little reluctance and get out of the house, Lionel.
explanation.walkthrough: Lionel Shriver is the novelist; take her surname and remove R.
explanation.definitionFit: To quiver or tremble, as with cold, is to shake.

clue.text: Uncivilized romantic lead with scar cut a dash

indicators.note: cut means removed, so the scar is taken away from the hero's name

parts.note: Heathcliff is the brooding hero of Wuthering Heights
a scar is a rocky cliff, a sense common in northern England
an en is a short dash in printing, the en dash

explanation.surface: A wild romantic hero with a scar still cut a dashing figure.
explanation.walkthrough: A scar in the Yorkshire Dales is a cliff, so cutting CLIFF leaves HEATH; add EN.
explanation.definitionFit: A heathen was once thought of as a barbarous unbeliever, so the word came to mean uncivilized.

clue.text: To her family, Brick Lane writer announced this pseudonym

indicators.note: announced means spoken out, so the writer's first name is heard

parts.note: Monica Ali wrote the novel Brick Lane

explanation.surface: The author of Brick Lane revealed the pen name her family know her by.
explanation.walkthrough: Monica Ali's first name, said aloud, gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A moniker is a name or nickname, close to an assumed name.

clue.text: Agonise badly after cutting start and end of Gunga Din

indicators.note: badly means in a mess, so the letters are rearranged
the start and end of a word are its first and last letters

explanation.surface: Agonising over a mangled reading of Kipling's poem Gunga Din.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Din' looks like part of Kipling's title, but it is the definition. Remove G and A (from Gunga) from AGONISE, as 'after cutting' says, and 'badly' rearranges what remains.
explanation.definitionFit: A din is a loud racket, a clamour of sound.

clue.text: "Everything exists, nothing has —" (E. M. Forster, A Passage To India)

definitions.text: "Everything exists, nothing has —" (E. M. Forster, A Passage To India)

parts.words: "Everything exists, nothing has —" (E. M. Forster, A Passage To India)
parts.note: a quotation with a gap to fill: in the Marabar Caves echo, Mrs Moore feels that nothing matters or counts for anything

explanation.definitionFit: The missing word means worth, the quality the line says nothing has.

clue.text: More than one funny bit of poetry penned by effervescent Rosen

indicators.note: penned by means enclosed by, so the line goes inside the other letters
effervescent means bubbling, so the letters of the name fizz into a new order

parts.note: a line is a bit of a poem

explanation.surface: Lots of laughs in the lively verse of Michael Rosen, the children's poet.
explanation.walkthrough: Michael Rosen is a much-loved British children's poet, and 'funny' here is a noun, a joke.
explanation.definitionFit: A funny is a joke, and the answer names short jokes, several of them.

clue.text: "Perhaps the — and simple pleasure of being seen for what one is compensates for the misery of being it" (Margaret Drabble, A Summer Bird-Cage)

definitions.text: "Perhaps the — and simple pleasure of being seen for what one is compensates for the misery of being it" (Margaret Drabble, A Summer Bird-Cage)

parts.words: "Perhaps the — and simple pleasure of being seen for what one is compensates for the misery of being it" (Margaret Drabble, A Summer Bird-Cage)
parts.note: a quotation with a gap to fill: the missing word describes a pleasure that is uncommon

explanation.definitionFit: The missing word means seldom found, uncommon.

clue.text: Nervously struggles free of leader, getting crafty

indicators.note: free of its leader means losing its first letter

parts.note: to wrestle is to struggle
sly means crafty or cunning

explanation.surface: A captive struggles to break free from the gang boss with some crafty moves.
explanation.walkthrough: WRESTLES without its first letter gives RESTLES; add SLY.
explanation.definitionFit: To act restlessly is to fidget in an uneasy, jumpy way.
